parakeet: Choosing your own path was cast as rebellion. As a result, exercising autonomy triggers the same emotional alarms that once accompanied sin, even after that belief has collapsed. This is the reversal that makes post-Christian life so difficult to navigate for some. Actions that are necessary for healthy adulthood, setting boundaries, revising beliefs, prioritizing personal agency, carry an inheritant sense of guilt and danger. The body and mind respond as though a line has been crossed, not because harm has occurred, but because the moral reflexes were conditioned under a framework where obedience was goodness and independence was disobedience. Reclaiming autonomy, then is not just an intellectual shift. It requires unlearning the emotional penalties attached to self-authorship. Christianity does not merely ask for belief, it asks for the surrender of the self. At its core, the system does not aim to cultivate confident moral agents, but compliant ones. When people are taught to distrust their own minds, bodies, and moral instincts, the outcome is not deeper wisdom or greater virtue. It's obedience. And obedience, however orderly it may appear, is not the same thing as ethical maturity or human flourishing. And this is the part we rarely name. These teachings don't stop shaping people when belief ends.
